client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time I try to sit down and focus on work, these memories of her just come flooding in and I can't concentrate on anything. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because nothing's really going to change the fact that she's gone.
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds really heavy — grief has a way of making even ordinary moments feel impossible, and it makes complete sense that your mind keeps returning to her. You're right that nothing will change the loss itself, and I want to honor that truth rather than gloss over it; but sometimes talking can help us find a way to *hold* the grief so it doesn't have to hold us hostage. I'm wondering — when those memories come flooding in, what kinds of thoughts tend to follow them?

client: Usually the thoughts are things like, "I should have called her more" or "I wasted so much time not visiting when I had the chance." And then I just feel this awful guilt sitting on my chest, like I failed her somehow. It's hard to shake because part of me genuinely believes those things are true, not just distorted thinking or whatever.
therapist: That guilt sounds like a real weight pressing down on you, and I want to gently acknowledge that it makes sense you'd feel that way — love often shows up *as* regret after a loss. In CBT we don't try to dismiss those thoughts as "just distorted," but we do ask whether they're telling the *complete* story — so I'm curious, when you think about the relationship you actually had with your grandmother, what do you think *she* would say about the time and care you gave her?

client: I think she would probably say something kind, that she knew I loved her and that I did what I could. But honestly, that almost makes it worse, because it feels like I'm just putting words in her mouth to make myself feel better, you know? Like I'm not sure I can trust that thought when the guilt feels so much more real and solid than any reassurance I try to give myself.
therapist: That's a really honest and thoughtful observation — you're essentially questioning your own reassurance, which shows how deeply the guilt has dug in. But I'd gently push back on one thing: the fact that guilt feels more *solid* doesn't necessarily mean it's more *accurate* — intense emotions can feel like evidence, but feeling guilty and actually having failed someone are two different things. What concrete things, however small, did you actually do that showed her you loved her?

client: I mean, I did call her on her birthday every year without fail, and when she was in the hospital two years ago I took time off work to be there with her. I guess there are real things I did, but my brain immediately jumps to "yeah but that's not enough, you could have done more." It's like no matter what I list, the guilt just moves the goalposts and finds a new reason why I still fell short.
therapist: You just named something really important — you can see the goalposts moving in real time, which means part of you recognizes this guilt isn't playing fair with you. That pattern, where no evidence is ever "enough," is actually a really common way grief keeps us stuck, because it's not really about the specific actions anymore — it's become a way of staying connected to her, even painfully. I'm wondering, do you think there's a part of you that's afraid that if you let go of the guilt, you might somehow lose your connection to her?

client: That actually stopped me for a second, because I hadn't thought about it that way. But I'm not sure I fully buy it either, because it feels a bit too neat, like a therapy explanation that sounds good but might not actually apply to me specifically. At the same time, I can't completely dismiss it, because the idea of just... moving on and feeling okay does feel kind of terrifying, like it would mean she didn't matter enough to keep hurting over.
therapist: I really appreciate your honesty in pushing back on that — you don't have to accept any explanation just because it sounds tidy, and your skepticism is actually healthy. But notice what you just said: that feeling *okay* feels terrifying because it might mean she didn't matter enough — that's not a therapy explanation, that's your own words describing something real in you. What if staying connected to her and gradually feeling less pain weren't actually opposites — is there another way you could imagine honoring how much she mattered that doesn't require keeping yourself in this much hurt?

client: I guess maybe there could be, like keeping some of her recipes and actually cooking them, or looking at photos sometimes without it turning into a spiral. But I'll be honest, even imagining doing those things feels really distant right now, like I intellectually understand what you're pointing at but emotionally I'm not there yet. I'm worried that if I try to do something like that too soon it'll just feel hollow, or worse, like I'm performing grief instead of actually feeling it.
therapist: The fact that you can even imagine those things — the recipes, the photos — is actually meaningful, even if it feels distant right now, and I want to honor that you're not ready yet rather than push you toward something that doesn't feel real. Your worry about it feeling hollow or performed makes a lot of sense, and I think it points to something important: you want your grief to be *genuine*, which itself is a form of love and respect for her. I'm wondering, what do you think "actually feeling it" looks like for you right now — is there a way you're already honoring her that you might not be giving yourself credit for?

client: Honestly, maybe the fact that I'm sitting here talking about her, that I can't stop thinking about her, that I care this much about whether I did enough... maybe that is something. I hadn't really framed it that way, I think I've been so focused on what I didn't do that I haven't considered that this whole painful process might itself be a way of honoring her. It's a small shift but it doesn't feel completely hollow when I say it, which surprises me a little.
therapist: That shift you just noticed — small as it feels — is actually really significant, because it came from *you*, not from me handing you a reframe. The fact that it doesn't feel hollow is important information worth trusting. I'm curious, as you sit with that idea for a moment, what does it feel like to consider that your love for her might be showing up *in* the grief rather than being something you have to prove despite it?

client: It feels... quieter, somehow, when I think about it that way, like some of the pressure lifts just slightly. I've been treating the grief like a problem to solve or a sign of failure, and the idea that it might just be love with nowhere to go right now is something I can actually sit with. I'm still scared it won't stick, that tomorrow I'll wake up and the guilt will just be back full force and this moment won't mean anything, but right now it feels real.
therapist: That quieter feeling you're describing right now is real, and it matters — even if the guilt comes back tomorrow, which it very well might, that doesn't erase what you just touched on in this moment. Grief doesn't tend to transform in one conversation, but these small moments of clarity are like footholds; you've found this perspective once, which means you can find your way back to it. As you go into the rest of your week, I'm wondering if there's one tiny thing you could do to gently remind yourself of it — even just a few words written down somewhere — so it has somewhere to live outside of this room?

client: I like the idea in theory, but I'm a little skeptical about writing things down because every time I've tried journaling or affirmations in the past it's ended up feeling forced and I just stop doing it after a day or two. I guess what feels more natural is maybe just saying it out loud to myself, something like "this is love with nowhere to go," because that phrasing actually landed for me in a way that felt true rather than like a motivational poster. I'm still not fully confident it'll help when the guilt hits hard, but it feels like something I might actually do rather than something I'd abandon out of guilt for not doing it right.
therapist: It's really wise that you know yourself well enough to skip what hasn't worked and go straight to what actually fits — that phrase belonging to *you*, coming from your own words in this conversation, makes it so much more likely to land when you need it. There's something almost poetic about speaking it out loud too, like you're giving voice to her in a way. I'm curious — can you imagine a moment this week when the guilt starts to rise, and what it might feel like to quietly say that to yourself in that moment?

client: Yeah, I can actually picture it pretty clearly — it'll probably be at my desk when I'm trying to work and a memory of her just cuts through everything, which has been happening almost every day. I think in that moment saying it out loud might feel a bit strange or even embarrassing, like I'm talking to myself, but maybe that's okay because it would at least interrupt the spiral before it takes over completely. I'm not promising myself it'll work, but I think I'm willing to try it once and see what happens, which is more than I could have said an hour ago.
therapist: There's something really meaningful in what you just said — an hour ago you weren't sure talking would help at all, and now you're willing to try something, on your own terms, in your own words. That's not a small thing. And I'd gently reframe the "talking to yourself" worry — in that moment at your desk, you won't really be talking to yourself, you'll be talking to her, and to the love that's still looking for somewhere to go. How are you feeling as we close out today, compared to where you started?
